records.text: Agile Compass for maturity in agile teams The Agile Compass checklist can help development teams identify which outcomes they have accomplished Practices learning Team conduct Pace of deliveries Features disclosure Software product Customer relationship Organisation support Credit: Agile Compass: A Tool for Identifying Maturity in Agile Software-Development Teams The Agile Compass checklist Agile Compass: Agile maturity models: a map, not the territory (and often a detour) Practices learning Beginning to try agile The team is trying to use an agile method with empirical learning. Most of times, not all practices were implemented. Benefits are not fully realised. We are learning on the fly We did not realise the expected benefits of agile adoption We are still learning how to deliver value to our customer Learning about agile The team is learning the agile method. The method is used "by the book" usually by getting training or coaching. Practices are fully implemented, as described in books and tutorials. It is important for the team to learn the value of each practice to be able to, later, tailor or even abandon them. We are following an agile method "by the book" We are getting training or coaching We are working with pilot projects Making sense of work processes The team understands agile practices and the value they add. They can now tailor the practices to their context and feel secure to be flexible in work processes, without abandoning agility. We learned the agile method and understand the value of each practice We are currently tailoring the practices We feel the work processes are more flexible according to the characteristics of each project Comprehending the situation The team has information about the work they perform. Information is simple and usually based on physical visibility or simple metrics. They use this information to make decisions and implement improvements in the process. These improvements are usually small and incremental. We are able to explain what happens in our work processes We have some metrics We use our understanding to make decisions Team conduct Responsive team The team needs close leadership to drive activities. They do not have/were given autonomy to make decisions. The team does not have the confidence to protect their work, that is, overtime is usual because of extra demands. We have partial autonomy to make decisions (about design, technology, project etc.) We feel the need to have the Scrum Master with us most of the time We have weak politics to protect team work Confident team This team still needs the Scrum Master around, but feel secure to make little decisions mainly about the project. Their communication is fluent. Changes in work processes need to be approved by management. We are fluent with practices and feel autonomous to some decisions in the project We know each other and are free to communicate We suggest improvements in the process, but they usually need approval Assertive team This team feels responsible for the project. They also have the autonomy to change the process. They make their own decisions and inform management. We have the autonomy to improve our work processes We have the capability to drive our own work during the project We have politics to protect our work Team leads continuous improvement This team is focused on technical excellence. They create their work processes, supported by management. They need a supportive environment to continue learning and, thus, motivated. It is possible to feel the focus on improving constantly. We define our work processes and change them whenever needed We feel highly motivated to continue learning We feel leadership supporting the implementation of our ideas Pace of deliveries Code finished at end of sprint Sprints are planned to finish code and integrate in repository. Most of times, functionality is not tested yet. The team is learning how to deliver value in the end of the sprint. In the end of the sprint, we have code finished, but we do not deliver it Our sprint size sometimes varies We are not sure of what adds value to our customer Functionality finished at end of sprint This team identifies the value to be delivered but cannot deliver in the end of the sprint. The environment is not fully supportive for agile build and code integration. Test is usually manual. We are capable of having functionalities ready to deliver in the end of the sprint, but we do not deliver We can identify a minimum releasable product Deliveries usually late Deliveries are planned and done, but usually late. Sometimes extra demands appear and the team has to address them. Environment is more supportive for automated build and integration. We plan our deliveries and do it, usually late Our stories sizes vary Deliveries done by deadline Deliveries are planned and done within deadline, sometimes before. Stories are usually small. Environment supports automated build and integration. We plan our deliveries and do them, sometimes before deadline. Our stories sizes are similar, usually small Features disclosure Requirements gathering Requirements are defined in the beginning of the project, usually with texts or diagrams. The team does not feel comfortable with changes or emerging requirements during the project. We define most of the requirements in the beginning of the project We do not know exactly how to deal with changes in requirements during the project Requirements discovery Requirements are vaguely defined in the beginning of the project, and detailed as sprints are initiated. Changes and emergent requirements are welcome. Spykes might be used for requirements elicitation. We define with details the requirements for the next sprint We are comfortable with changes or emergent requirements We can identify a minimum releasable product in our stories Requirements quality There are clear initiatives to guarantee the quality of the requirements, for them to be in accordance to customer needs. We are concerned with whether what we deliver to our customer is exactly what the customer needs We endeavor initiatives to improve the quality of the requirements Software product High-level source code Coding is an important activity and there are initiatives to guarantee the code is clear and robust, using best-practices available. We care about our code We endeavor initiatives to guarantee our code is fine, such as reviews, refactoring, pair programming or others Awareness of failures There are failures in deliveries that need to be treated as soon as possible, as well as failures happen because of problems in development process We spend some time in the sprint correcting bugs from the previous sprint We spend some time in the sprint with issues in code building and integration High-level software There is a concern with the quality of the feature being delivered. For this reason, test is a priority, either automated or not. Also, there is a concern with the integrity of the code in repository. We see test as a priority Code is integrated as soon as possible Our code repository is always healthy Efficient coding Coding, integration and testing is performed with an infrastructure that allows agility. The team is concerned with removing unnecessary delays in work processes. Devops is a common infrastructure to allow efficient coding. We have automated tests, either unit or functional tests Our build and integration are automated We are concerned with removing delays in work processes, by automating manual tasks Customer relationship Team awareness of customer The team is learning how the customer business is and the demands dynamics. This is the reason their contribution to customer requirements is still incipient. We are getting to know our customer and the demands We have partial ability to help customer defining requirements Customer awareness of team It is the learning process of the customer about the team. The customer is getting to know the processes, but is not fully used to that. Sometimes it seems there is a lack of trust on the team. Our customer is learning how we work The customer knows what we are going to deliver The customer is not fully comfortable about reprioritizing requirements Confident customer The customer is confident about team's work. He trusts the team is concerned about delivering what he needs. The customer is usually more flexible about deliveries and is more comfortable with reprioritizing requirements. There is transparency between the team and the customer. We assist customer in requirements definition Customer is aware of its role in the process We feel the customer trusts our work Partner customer The customer recognises the partnership with the team: while he feels the team is committed with his business, the team feels the customer as being part of the team. We identify and suggest improvements for our customer business Our customer feels as begin part of our team, with shared responsibility about deliveries Organisation support A few teams using agile Some isolated teams are starting to work with agile. The company knows, but is not concerned in acknowledging the process or the results. We see isolated agile initiatives in our company We feel weak acknowledgment of top management about these initiatives Agile commitment Top management decided to implement agile in the company and initiatives are official. There are investments with training, coaching, communication and infrastructure for agile transformation. There are official agile pilot projects in the company We feel company support (training, coaching or infrastructure) for agile transformation Agile priority There is full support from top management for agile transformation. Departments, roles, teams change to support agility. When it is a top-bottom initiative, resistance still appears in some teams. We see that the company' structure (physical and departmental) has changed to support agile transformation We feel there is some resistance to change in some teams Agile business Software development companies that are created with agile methods are, usually, agile businesses. The company management strategies are focused on people and leanness, not just for software development, but for the whole company. Our whole company is recognised as being agile Our teams adopt an agile foundation, but customise the way they work according to the projects characteristics

records.text: Agile Fluency See Agile Fluency by James Shore and Diana Larsen One-Star Teams Create Business Value Benefit: Greater visibility into teams’ work; ability to redirect. Investment: Team development and work process design. Core Metric: Team regularly reports progress from a business value perspective. Transparency: Management knows when the team is building the wrong thing, or isn’t making progress, and has the ability to positively intervene. Alignment: The team works collaboratively, reducing misunderstanding and hand-off delays. Two-Star Teams Deliver on the Market’s Cadence Benefit: Low defects and high productivity. Investment: Lowered productivity during technical skill development. Core Metric: Team ships on market cadence. Transparency: Fast concept-to-delivery cycle times reveal systemic flaws early. Alignment: High technical quality and frequent delivery results in high morale, and more productive work. Three-Star Teams Optimise Their Value Benefit: Higher value deliveries and better product decisions. Investment: Social capital expended on incorporating business expertise into team. Core Metric: Team provides concrete business metrics. Transparency: The team reports its results using concrete business metrics, such as RoI, net profit per employee, and customer satisfaction. Alignment: Mutual trust between the team and its organisation leads to rapid, effective negotiation, and the team’s broad-based expertise eliminates hand-offs and speeds decision making. Four-Star Teams Contribute to Optimising the System Benefit: Alignment with organisational goals; synergistic effects. Investment: Significant effort in establishing organisational culture; inventing new practices. Core Metric: Team reports how its actions impact the overall organisation. Transparency: The team describes its work in the context of the business’s other initiatives, allowing products to be balanced against each other. Alignment: The team cross-pollinates perspectives, context, and innovations with other teams and other parts of the organisation.

headings: AI Maturity Model for a National Health Service
records.text: AI Maturity Model for a National Health Service Disclaimer: This page is generated by AI. This information is intended for general purpose eduction and for a generic national health service, and is NOT for production use, NOT for any specific national health service, and NOT for any medical purpose. Contents: Maturity model levels How to use this model Developer tooling Automatic testing Software architecture Software quality assurance Software high availability Software disaster recovery Software DevOps Cloud services capabilities Cloud services FinOps User-Centered Design (UCD/UI/UX) AI in our software products AI in our medical devices Integrations with EHR, EMR, etc. Vendor capabilities Ambient scribes Hospital administration General practice administration Compliance department Finance department Legal department Human resources department Public relations department Cybersecurity Apps and websites for patients Apps and websites for providers System leadership of software engineering System leadership of medical practitioners System leadership of government stakeholders Digital sovereignty Upskilling Redundancies Notes on scope Citations Citations by practice area Maturity model levels Level 0: None, Never, Negligible, Not Applicable. Level 1: Initiate, Investigate, Implicit, Individual-oriented, Informal-usage. Level 2: Develop, Describe, Duplicate, Direct-oriented, Department-usage. Level 3: Standardise, Specify, Scale, Service-oriented, Segment-usage. Level 4: Manage, Measure, Mainstream, Mission-oriented, Mass-usage. Level 5: Orchestrate, Optimise, Originate, Opportunity-oriented, Outsize-usage. How to use this model Score each practice area independently. A health service is typically level 4 in one area and level 1 in another, and that unevenness is the useful signal. Score what is evidenced, not what is aspired to. If a control exists but produces no artifact, treat it as the level below. Read the levels as cumulative. Level 4 assumes the level 3 standards still hold, and level 5 assumes the level 4 measures still run. Treat regulated areas differently. For clinical and device practice areas, a jump from level 1 to level 3 without the intervening governance work is a safety risk, not a shortcut. Re-score on a fixed cadence, such as annually, so the model measures trajectory rather than a single moment. Developer tooling Level 0: None. No AI assistance exists in the software development toolchain, either because it was never considered or because it is blocked outright with no route to approval. Engineers write, review, and refactor entirely unaided. Network policy blocks all public model endpoints and no exception process exists. No AI coding assistant licenses have ever been purchased. No policy statement exists, so teams assume a ban and self-censor. Level 1: Initiate. Individual engineers experiment on their own initiative, often on personal accounts and outside procurement. Usage is invisible to the organisation and creates unmanaged data-leakage exposure. A developer pastes a non-clinical utility function into a consumer chatbot to get a refactor. One squad shares useful prompts in a group chat with no retention or review. No telemetry exists, so leadership cannot say how many staff use AI tooling. Level 2: Develop. One or two departments buy seats and write a short internal usage note. Practice is described and duplicated team by team rather than being consistent across the organisation. A digital directorate buys a licence pool for its own engineers only. A wiki page states never to paste patient-identifiable data into a prompt. Each repository carries its own hand-copied prompt or rules file. Level 3: Standardise. A single approved toolchain is specified for all engineering: enterprise identity, in-jurisdiction hosting, logging, and an approved model list. AI-assisted code follows the same review, security, and clinical-safety gates as any other code. Assistants are accessed only through single sign-on with per-user audit logging and no training on submitted code. A standard repository rules file encodes coding standards, secure-coding rules, and banned patterns. Secret scanning and dependency provenance checks run on every AI-assisted pull request. Level 4: Manage. Adoption and quality are measured, not assumed. AI tooling is mainstream across all engineering teams, and its controls are audited on the same cycle as other information-governance controls. Dashboards track suggestion acceptance rate, review time, and post-merge defect rate for AI-assisted changes. Commit metadata records AI assistance so defect trends can be compared against unassisted work. An annual internal audit samples AI-assisted changes for licence, security, and safety compliance. Level 5: Orchestrate. The organisation runs its own grounded developer platform, tuned to its codebases, clinical-safety standards, and information-governance rules, and it exports that capability to peer organisations. An internal agent is grounded on the organisation's own repositories, architecture decisions, and coding standards. Automated agents draft clinical-safety and data-protection checklists as part of the pull-request template. Reusable toolchain configurations are published to other trusts, boards, and regional bodies for reuse. Automatic testing Level 0: None. Testing is manual or minimal, and AI plays no part in producing or maintaining tests. Regression risk is carried by people re-running scripts by hand. Release testing is a manual checklist executed by a QA analyst. No continuous integration pipeline runs tests on every change. Test data is a stale copy with no defined refresh or masking process. Level 1: Initiate. An individual uses AI to draft a handful of tests for code they happen to be working on. There is no expectation that anyone else does the same. A developer generates unit tests for a single service and commits them unreviewed. Generated tests assert current behaviour rather than intended behaviour, locking in bugs. No one tracks which tests were AI-generated. Level 2: Develop. A team adopts a described convention for AI-assisted test generation and copies it to neighbouring teams. Coverage improves in pockets, and synthetic test data starts to be discussed as a governance question. A team standard requires a human to review and rename every generated test before merge. A department generates synthetic patient records for testing rather than using masked live extracts. A shared prompt template produces tests in the team's chosen assertion style. Level 3: Standardise. Test generation, test data, and test review are specified organisation-wide and enforced in the pipeline. Test evidence is fit to reference from a clinical risk file where the software touches care. Pipelines fail builds below a defined coverage and mutation-score threshold regardless of how tests were authored. One officer reviews a single AI pilot as a favour with no defined criteria. Guidance is given verbally in meetings and never written down. There is no escalation route when an officer is unsure. Level 2: Develop. The department writes an AI policy and keeps a list of known systems. Coverage is partial and depends on teams volunteering that they are using AI. An acceptable-use policy for generative AI is published to staff. A manually maintained list of AI initiatives is compiled from a survey. Data-protection impact assessments gain an AI annex. Level 3: Standardise. A specified AI management system governs the lifecycle: risk tiering, mandatory impact assessments, approval gates, human-oversight requirements, transparency records, and defined roles and accountabilities. An AI management system aligned to a recognised standard defines policy, roles, risk tiering, and review cycles. Data-protection and equality impact assessments are mandatory gates before any AI go-live. A central AI register records purpose, risk tier, owner, oversight design, and review date for every system. Level 4: Manage. Controls are measured for effectiveness rather than existence. Monitoring is continuous, internal audit tests the controls, and the board receives regular AI risk reporting. Control effectiveness metrics such as assessment completion and overdue review rates are reported monthly. Internal audit performs an independent AI governance audit on a defined cycle. An AI oversight committee reviews incidents, drift alerts, and exception requests with authority to suspend systems. Level 5: Orchestrate. Compliance operates as an enabling service with automated evidence collection, and the organisation engages regulators early rather than reactively. Evidence for assurance is collected automatically from pipelines and monitoring rather than assembled by hand. Pre-approved patterns let low-risk use cases self-certify in days rather than months. The organisation participates in regulatory sandboxes and contributes to national guidance. Finance department Level 0: None. Finance uses no AI. Ledger work, forecasting, and procurement analysis are entirely manual or rule-based. Invoice matching is fully manual. Budget forecasting is spreadsheet extrapolation of prior-year actuals. No anomaly detection runs over transactions. Level 1: Initiate. An individual accountant uses a general-purpose model for personal productivity. Nothing is validated and nothing is shared. An analyst asks a model to write a complex spreadsheet formula. A manager drafts a business case narrative with AI and edits it lightly. Financial figures are pasted into an unapproved tool. Level 2: Develop. The department pilots one automation with described scope and controls, usually in transaction processing. Benefits are local and manually verified. Invoice coding is automated for a single supplier category with full manual review. A pilot flags duplicate payments for human investigation. Results are checked by re-performing the work manually for the pilot period. Level 3: Standardise. AI is specified within the standard financial control environment: segregation of duties, approval thresholds, audit trails, and explainability sufficient for external audit. Purchase-to-pay automation operates within documented approval limits and cannot approve its own exceptions. Every AI-influenced posting carries a traceable audit trail showing inputs, model version, and approver. Forecasting models are documented with assumptions, limitations, and sensitivity analysis for auditors. Level 4: Manage. Finance measures the value and the risk. AI is mainstream in month-end, forecasting, and counter-fraud, and its accuracy and savings are reported rather than asserted. Forecast accuracy, exception rates, and realised savings are reported to the finance committee. Counter-fraud analytics are measured on detection rate and false-positive burden, not alert volume. The total cost of AI itself, including inference, licensing, and staff time, is tracked as a managed cost line. Level 5: Orchestrate. Finance orchestrates planning and investment decisions across the organisation, and treats AI capability as a portfolio to be optimised rather than a set of purchases. Scenario planning models the financial effect of demand, workforce, and policy changes simultaneously. AI investment decisions use a standard value framework including patient outcomes and staff time released. Continuous cost optimisation shifts workloads between models and providers against measured quality thresholds. Legal department Level 0: None. Legal work is entirely manual. Contracts, advice, and inquest support are produced without AI assistance. Contract review is a full manual read of every clause. Precedents live in individual lawyers' folders. No legal-technology tooling is in place. Level 1: Initiate. An individual lawyer uses a public chatbot for first drafts, exposing the organisation to confidentiality risk and fabricated citations. A draft response is produced with a consumer tool and contains an invented case citation. Confidential material is pasted into a service with unclear retention. No verification step is required before the draft is used. Level 2: Develop. The department buys a legal AI tool and describes verification rules. Use is confined to the legal team and depends on individual discipline. A tool is licensed for contract summarisation with a rule that all citations must be checked. A short internal note describes what may and may not be entered into the tool. Privileged material handling is discussed but not technically enforced. Level 3: Standardise. A specified approach covers tooling, confidentiality, privilege, retention, and verification, and legal owns the AI clause library the whole organisation uses in procurement. Retrieval is grounded on the organisation's own precedents and policies, with citations linked to source documents. Privileged and confidential material is technically segregated with enforced retention and no vendor training. A standard AI clause set covers liability, model change notification, data use, indemnity, and exit. Level 4: Manage. Legal measures throughput and quality, and AI is mainstream across contracting, advice, and case support. Verification remains mandatory and is audited. Contract cycle time, clause deviation rates, and rework rates are tracked and reported. Sampling audits confirm every AI-assisted output was verified before release. Inquest and claims preparation uses AI to assemble chronologies from records under lawyer review. Level 5: Orchestrate. Legal orchestrates horizon scanning and risk strategy, turning regulatory change into organisational action quickly, and contributes to shared national legal assets. Automated horizon scanning maps new AI and health regulation to affected internal policies and systems. An AI liability strategy covers clinical negligence, product liability, and supplier apportionment explicitly. The department co-authors model contract terms shared with peer organisations nationally. Human resources department Level 0: None. HR uses no AI. Recruitment, workforce planning, and case management are entirely manual, and no AI workforce strategy exists. Job adverts and shortlisting are fully manual. Workforce planning is headcount extrapolation in a spreadsheet. No AI literacy content exists in the training catalogue. Level 1: Initiate. Individual managers use general-purpose models informally for writing tasks. There is no policy, and staff are unsure whether it is allowed. A manager drafts a job advert and a person specification with a consumer tool. Someone summarises anonymised interview notes with an unapproved application. Staff receive contradictory verbal advice on what is permitted. Level 2: Develop. HR pilots one use case and documents the concerns, particularly bias and lawfulness of automated decision-making. Practice is described but not yet controlled organisation-wide. A screening tool is piloted for one high-volume role with full human review of every rejection. Candidate-facing wording about AI involvement is drafted for that pilot. Bias testing is discussed but not yet performed on real applicant data. Level 3: Standardise. Specified rules govern all AI in employment decisions: no solely automated adverse decision, mandatory equality impact assessment, bias testing, candidate transparency, and appeal routes. Staff AI literacy becomes a defined curriculum. Policy requires a human decision-maker with genuine authority for every rejection, sanction, or dismissal. Equality impact assessment and pre-deployment bias testing are mandatory before any hiring tool goes live. A role-based AI training curriculum covers clinical, administrative, and technical staff. Level 4: Manage. HR measures fairness and effect, not just adoption. AI is mainstream across recruitment and workforce planning, and adverse impact is monitored continuously. Adverse impact ratios by protected characteristic are monitored at each recruitment stage and reported. Time to hire, offer acceptance, and early attrition are tracked against pre-AI baselines. AI capability is a named element of appraisal and workforce capability frameworks. Level 5: Orchestrate. HR orchestrates workforce strategy around changing roles, using skills-based planning and continuous fairness auditing, and shapes the wider workforce agenda. Skills-based planning models how AI changes role composition and redeploys staff rather than displacing them. Internal mobility matching surfaces opportunities to existing staff before external recruitment opens. Independent fairness audits are commissioned and their findings published internally. Public relations department Level 0: None. Communications uses no AI. All content, translation, and media monitoring is produced manually. Press releases and campaign copy are written entirely by hand. Translation is outsourced with long turnaround times. Media and social monitoring is manual searching. Level 1: Initiate. An individual communications officer drafts posts with a general-purpose model. There is no disclosure practice and no check on clinical accuracy. A social post about a service change is drafted by AI and published with light editing. An AI-generated image is used without any provenance labelling. No one checks whether health claims in the copy are clinically accurate. Level 2: Develop. The department writes a style guide covering AI drafting and describes when disclosure is required. Practice is consistent inside communications but not beyond it. A style guide states AI may draft but never approve, and a named human owns every publication. Synthetic imagery requires internal labelling and sign-off. Health-related copy must be reviewed by a clinician before release. Level 3: Standardise. Specified standards apply to all AI-assisted communication: approved tools, provenance labelling of synthetic media, clinical sign-off for health claims, accessibility and reading-age standards, and defined escalation. Provenance metadata and visible labelling are applied to all synthetic or substantially AI-generated media. Every public health message passes an accessibility and reading-age check before release. Multilingual output is produced through an assured translation route with human review for clinical content. Level 4: Manage. Communications is measured on reach, comprehension, and trust, and AI is mainstream across campaigns, media handling, and correspondence. Reading age, comprehension testing, and translation quality are measured per campaign. Response times for enquiries and complaints correspondence are tracked with AI-assisted drafting in place. Sentiment and trust indicators are monitored across communities, not only in aggregate. Level 5: Orchestrate. Communications orchestrates real-time public engagement, including misinformation detection and rebuttal, and co-produces content with patients and communities. Health misinformation is detected across channels and rebuttal content is prepared for rapid human approval. Crisis simulations rehearse AI-assisted response including deepfake and impersonation scenarios. Patients and community groups co-produce messaging, with AI used to adapt tone and format per audience. Cybersecurity Level 0: None. Security does not consider AI at all, neither as a defensive tool nor as a new attack surface. AI systems, if any exist, are outside the security perimeter and outside the asset register. No threat model covers models, prompts, training data, or inference endpoints. Model and vector-database endpoints produce no security logs. Phishing awareness material makes no mention of AI-generated lures or synthetic voice. Level 1: Initiate. An individual analyst experiments with AI for alert triage while unsanctioned AI use spreads unmonitored elsewhere in the organisation. Nobody can quantify the exposure. A security analyst pastes log extracts into a consumer chatbot to summarise an incident. Shadow AI usage is suspected but no discovery has been run. AI appears nowhere on the corporate or cyber risk register. Level 2: Develop. The security team describes rules for AI-assisted work and pilots one detection use case. Coverage is departmental and AI-specific threats are acknowledged but not yet controlled. A pilot applies behavioural analytics to identity and access telemetry in one domain. A shadow-AI discovery exercise produces a first inventory of model endpoints in use. AI risk is added to the risk register with an owner but no treatment plan. Level 3: Standardise. AI systems are brought fully inside the security framework, with AI-specific threat modelling, gateway controls, and supplier security requirements specified for every deployment. Every AI system has a threat model covering prompt injection, training-data poisoning, model and prompt exfiltration, and insecure output handling. Data-loss prevention, redaction, and rate limiting are enforced at the model gateway, not left to user discipline. AI assets are recorded in the configuration management database with owners, data classifications, and review dates, and are in scope of the national cyber assessment framework submission. Level 4: Manage. Security outcomes are measured, AI defensive tooling is mainstream in the security operations centre, and AI systems are red-teamed on a schedule rather than after an incident. Mean time to detect and respond is tracked before and after AI-assisted triage, with false-positive burden measured. Scheduled adversarial testing of deployed AI systems is contracted and its findings tracked to closure. Service desk identity verification is hardened against synthetic voice and deepfake impersonation, and tested. Level 5: Orchestrate. Detection, response, and threat intelligence are orchestrated across the health system, with supervised automation and rehearsed resilience against AI-enabled attacks. Containment playbooks execute automatically for defined high-confidence detections, with a human veto and full audit trail. AI threat intelligence is exchanged across organisations in the health system in near real time. Large-scale exercises rehearse AI-enabled ransomware and data-integrity attacks alongside clinical continuity plans. Apps and websites for patients Level 0: None. Patient-facing digital services contain no AI. Content is static, personalisation is absent, and every interaction that needs judgement goes to a telephone queue. Service information pages are hand-maintained static content. Booking and cancellation are telephone-only. No patient-facing search or navigation assistance exists. Level 1: Initiate. A team bolts a chatbot onto a website on its own initiative, without clinical review, accessibility testing, or an escalation path to a human. A generic question-answering widget is added to a service page overnight. The bot has no route to a human and no red-flag handling. No reading-age, translation, or accessibility check was performed. Level 2: Develop. A department pilots an AI-assisted patient journey with documented disclaimers, consent wording, and clinician oversight. Practice is local and inconsistently applied elsewhere. One service pilots AI-assisted appointment triage with every output reviewed by a clinician. Escalation from the digital route to a human is described in a local procedure. Accessibility issues are fixed retrospectively after user complaints. Level 3: Standardise. All patient-facing AI follows one specified standard: accessible to at least the recognised international level AA, clearly disclosed as AI-generated, safety-netted with hard routing of red flags to humans, assessed for data protection, and making no clinical claims unless properly regulated. AI-generated patient content is labelled as such and has a named human owner accountable for accuracy. Red-flag symptom patterns bypass the AI entirely and route directly to urgent clinical assessment. Translation into the most-used local languages is produced through an assured route with human review of clinical content. Level 4: Manage. Patient-facing AI is mainstream and measured on outcomes and equity, not on usage volume. Non-digital routes are deliberately maintained and monitored. Completion rates, satisfaction, and escalation appropriateness are broken down by age, deprivation, disability, and language. Reported harms and near misses from digital routes flow into the patient-safety incident system. Telephone and in-person routes are retained with measured parity of access and waiting time. Level 5: Orchestrate. Patient-facing services are orchestrated around the individual: personalised, proactive, co-produced with patients, integrated with the record and care plan, and continuously evaluated in public. Care plans and results are explained in plain language in the patient's preferred language and format. Proactive prompts for screening, vaccination, and long-term condition review are personalised and evaluated for equity. Patients control which data AI features may use, with the choice visible and revocable at any time. Apps and websites for providers Level 0: None. Staff-facing digital estate contains no AI. Policies and guidance sit in document stores that are hard to search and often out of date. Clinical guidelines are published as documents on an intranet with weak search. There is no single place to find the current formulary or pathway. No usage analytics exist for staff-facing content. Level 1: Initiate. Individual staff use consumer AI tools to answer clinical and operational questions, which risks confidently wrong guidance with no provenance. A clinician asks a consumer chatbot about a dosing question and receives an unsourced answer. Answers cannot be traced to any approved local policy or national guideline. No logging exists, so errors cannot be investigated afterwards. Level 2: Develop. A department deploys retrieval over its own approved documents and describes the caveats. It works well for that directorate and is not extended. A guideline search assistant is built over one directorate's policy library. Disclaimers and a feedback mechanism are described in a local procedure. Source documents are refreshed manually and drift out of date. Level 3: Standardise. A specified standard governs all staff-facing AI: grounded only on approved sources, every answer cited to a versioned document, role-based access, embedded in the workflow, and covered by a clinical safety case. Every answer links to the specific approved policy or guideline and its version and review date. Retrieval is restricted to a curated corpus, and out-of-corpus questions return an explicit refusal rather than a guess. Access is by single sign-on with per-user audit logging suitable for incident investigation. Level 4: Manage. Staff-facing AI is mainstream and its accuracy is audited rather than assumed. Content freshness is managed automatically and usage is measured against clinical benefit. A quarterly clinical accuracy audit samples answers and grades them against source guidance. Stale or superseded sources are automatically flagged, quarantined, and removed from retrieval. Time to find guidance, guideline adherence, and staff-reported usefulness are tracked. Level 5: Orchestrate. Provider tooling is orchestrated into clinical workflow, with agents that act in context, continuous knowledge curation, and content shared across organisations. Decision support appears at the point of ordering or prescribing rather than in a separate application. National or regional guideline changes propagate automatically to local pathways with change notification to affected staff. Curated knowledge and evaluation results are shared with peer organisations rather than rebuilt in each one. System leadership of software engineering Level 0: None. There is no engineering leadership. Software capability is entirely outsourced, and technical direction is set by whichever supplier is currently engaged. No executive is accountable for software engineering or technology strategy. No in-house engineering capability exists at any level. Architecture decisions are made in supplier proposals rather than by the organisation. Level 1: Initiate. A single champion pushes AI forward without mandate, budget, or succession. Progress depends entirely on that person staying. A head of development runs AI experiments alongside a full delivery workload. There is no funded roadmap, only opportunistic proofs of concept. If the champion leaves, nothing continues. Level 2: Develop. One department writes a strategy and a target architecture, and hires its own specialists. Other parts of the organisation take different directions. A directorate publishes an AI strategy that other directorates do not follow. A data science team is formed in one organisation with no shared platform. Skills gaps are described in a paper but not funded. Level 3: Standardise. An engineering operating model is specified across the organisation or region: platform teams, service ownership, architecture principles that include AI, and defined career paths. Architecture principles mandate a governed model gateway, an evaluation harness, and monitoring for any AI service. A platform team owns shared AI services so product teams do not each rebuild them. Engineering job families, progression, and pay bands are defined and published. Level 4: Manage. Engineering leadership is measured and accountable at board level. Delivery, capability, and build-versus-buy decisions are evidenced rather than asserted. Delivery metrics such as deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and restoration time are reported to the board. A named executive holds explicit accountability for AI outcomes and risks in the boardroom. Recruitment, retention, and internal capability growth are tracked against a workforce plan. Level 5: Orchestrate. Engineering leadership extends beyond the organisation. Shared platforms, open source, and talent pipelines are orchestrated across the health system, and the organisation sets direction rather than following it. A shared regional platform serves multiple organisations instead of each maintaining its own. Reusable components are open-sourced and their reuse by peers is tracked and supported. Apprenticeships, academic partnerships, and clinical-technical hybrid roles build a sustained pipeline. System leadership of medical practitioners Level 0: None. Clinicians have no leadership role in AI. Decisions are made by technology and procurement functions, and clinical risk ownership is undefined. No chief clinical or nursing information officer role exists. No certified clinical safety officer is appointed for digital deployments. Clinicians first learn about an AI tool when it appears in their workflow. Level 1: Initiate. An enthusiastic individual clinician advocates for AI without job-planned time, mandate, or a governance route. Their projects live and die with their goodwill. A consultant runs AI evaluations in their own unpaid time. There is no route from their project into clinical governance. Colleagues are unaware the work is happening. Level 2: Develop. A department appoints a digital clinical lead with described responsibilities and some protected time. Influence is limited to that department. A directorate clinical lead has job-planned sessions for digital work. A local route into the directorate governance meeting is described. One local training session on AI is delivered to a specialty team. Level 3: Standardise. Clinical digital leadership is specified organisation-wide, with named senior clinical information roles, certified clinical safety officers, AI standing in clinical governance, and explicit statements of professional accountability. A certified clinical safety officer with job-planned time is required for every AI deployment. AI performance and incidents are a standing item in clinical governance and clinical audit. Policy states plainly that clinical accountability for a decision stays with the clinician regardless of AI involvement. Level 4: Manage. Clinical leadership is measured on the things that matter: clinician confidence, appropriate reliance, override behaviour, training, and safety outcomes across the whole workforce. Automation-bias audits sample cases where clinicians agreed with and overrode AI output, and look for inappropriate deference. AI literacy is embedded in mandatory training, appraisal, and continuing professional development. Clinician-reported experience of AI tools is surveyed and acted on, with results published internally. Level 5: Orchestrate. Clinical leaders shape the field beyond their own organisation, through research, guideline development, professional standards, and evaluation networks. A clinical academic partnership prospectively evaluates deployed AI and publishes the results, including negative findings. Clinicians contribute to national guidelines and professional body positions on AI in practice. Clinical AI fellowships and secondments build a pipeline of clinically credible digital leaders. System leadership of government stakeholders Level 0: None. There is no engagement with government, regulators, or national bodies on AI. Public accountability for AI use is undefined. No reporting on AI reaches the sponsoring department or national body. The organisation does not respond to policy consultations. There is no funding strategy for AI beyond opportunistic bids. Level 1: Initiate. Individuals respond to consultations or talk to national contacts informally. Positions are personal and uncoordinated. One executive answers a call for evidence without internal sign-off. An informal relationship with a national programme lead is the only channel. Two parts of the organisation give national bodies contradictory information. Level 2: Develop. The organisation describes its position and briefs stakeholders occasionally, usually around a specific bid or visit. Engagement is reactive. A briefing pack is produced for a visiting politician or national official. A benefits case is written to support one national funding bid. The organisation joins a national pilot without a plan for what happens after it. Level 3: Standardise. Engagement is specified and routine: published transparency records, defined reporting lines to national bodies and regulators, board-level accountability for AI, and deliberate alignment to national strategy and funding conditions. Algorithmic transparency records are published for public-facing AI as a matter of standard practice. Reporting routes to the sponsoring department, the device regulator, and the data protection authority are defined and rehearsed. Local AI plans are explicitly mapped to national digital and data strategy commitments. Level 4: Manage. Performance is measured against national frameworks, benchmarked against peers, and subject to independent external scrutiny that the organisation can evidence. The organisation benchmarks itself through national digital maturity assessments and acts on the gaps. External audit and parliamentary or public scrutiny is met with prepared evidence rather than improvisation. An annual public report covers AI use, benefits, incidents, and equity impact. Level 5: Orchestrate. The organisation co-creates policy, standards, and funding models, works internationally, and helps shape the rules that everyone else will follow. Staff sit on regulator sandboxes, standards committees, and national advisory groups. International collaboration shares evaluation methods and real-world evidence across health systems. The organisation helps design national procurement frameworks and payment models for AI. Digital sovereignty Level 0: None. Where data is processed, who can access it, and under whose law is never asked. Defaults are whatever the supplier offers. Contracts contain no data residency or jurisdiction clause. Subprocessors and their locations are unknown and unlisted. Nobody can say which country a given inference request is served from. Level 1: Initiate. An individual raises the question and investigates informally. There is concern but no requirement, register, or decision. An architect asks a supplier where inference happens and receives a vague answer. A project notes an international data transfer without completing a transfer risk assessment. No register of cross-border data flows exists. Level 2: Develop. One department writes residency requirements into a single contract and drafts transfer assessments. Practice is duplicated case by case rather than set as policy. One contract requires in-country storage but is silent on processing and support access. A transfer risk assessment is drafted for a single supplier. A stated preference for local hosting exists with no enforcement mechanism. Level 3: Standardise. Sovereignty requirements are specified for every AI system: data residency, jurisdictional control, subprocessor transparency, key management, and evidenced portability and exit. Patient data is processed in-country under domestic law, including support and administrative access paths. Encryption keys are customer-managed and revocable, so a supplier cannot read data unilaterally. An approved model list records hosting location, jurisdiction, and retention terms for each option. Level 4: Manage. Sovereignty risk is measured and managed as a strategic risk: concentration, dependency, and lock-in are quantified and reported, and exit is rehearsed rather than theoretical. A live register records every cross-border transfer with its lawful basis and safeguards. Supplier and model concentration risk is quantified and reported to the board alongside other strategic risks. Exit and portability tests are executed on a schedule, including extraction of prompts, configurations, and fine-tuning assets. Level 5: Orchestrate. The organisation has genuine strategic autonomy. Workloads move between providers without service loss, open and sovereign options are viable, and shared public infrastructure reduces dependency. Critical AI workloads are proven portable across at least two providers with measured switch time. Open-weight models running on national or regional compute are validated as credible alternatives for defined use cases. The organisation contributes to and consumes shared public AI infrastructure rather than duplicating private stacks. Upskilling Level 0: None. No AI training exists. The workforce is unprepared, and nobody knows what the baseline skill level is. Induction and mandatory training contain no AI or data literacy content. No digital skills baseline has ever been measured. There is no training budget line for AI. Level 1: Initiate. Individuals teach themselves in their own time and at their own expense. Skill is concentrated in a few enthusiasts and invisible to workforce planning. A clinician completes an online AI course unfunded and outside working hours. Informal lunchtime sessions are run by whoever is interested. No record exists of who has been trained in what. Level 2: Develop. A department builds a curriculum for its own staff and tracks completion locally. Quality varies and nothing transfers between departments. A directorate runs AI awareness sessions for its own teams only. A local champions network forms without a defined role or time allocation. Completion is tracked in a spreadsheet held by the department. Level 3: Standardise. A role-based curriculum is specified for the whole workforce, with defined competencies, mandatory foundations, protected time, and assessment, aligned to recognised capability frameworks. Tiered pathways serve all staff, frequent users, builders, and approvers, each with defined competencies. AI and data literacy is part of induction and mandatory training for every role. Protected learning time is job-planned rather than expected to happen in gaps. Level 4: Manage. Capability is measured, not attendance. Competence, confidence, and safe applied use are assessed across the whole workforce and drive targeted intervention. Competence is assessed through practical scenarios, including recognising when not to trust an AI output. Capability data by staff group and site identifies where to invest next. Training coverage is correlated with AI-related incidents and unsafe-use reports. Level 5: Orchestrate. Learning is orchestrated as a continuous system embedded in work, with fellowships, academic partnerships, and curricula exported to the wider health system. In-workflow coaching surfaces guidance at the moment of use rather than in a classroom months earlier. AI fellowships and secondments rotate staff between clinical, technical, and governance roles. Curricula and assessment materials are shared with other organisations and education providers. Redundancies Level 0: None. Workforce impact is not considered. Business cases claim savings without stating whether posts are affected, and no consultation or redeployment thinking exists. An AI business case claims a cash-releasing saving without naming any affected role. No workforce impact assessment template exists. Staff representatives are not involved in AI decisions at any stage. Level 1: Initiate. Individual managers speculate and act informally. Anxiety spreads through rumour, which damages adoption more than the technology ever would. Rumours circulate that AI will cut administrative posts, with no official statement. A manager quietly freezes a vacancy in anticipation of automation. Staff hide their own AI use for fear of automating their own role away. Level 2: Develop. A department describes expected workforce impact in a business case and handles consequences case by case. Consultation starts late, after decisions are effectively made. A directorate business case states a number of posts released without specifying which roles or how. A few staff are redeployed informally through manager goodwill. Formal consultation begins only once the technology is already contracted. Level 3: Standardise. A specified policy requires workforce impact assessment before AI approval, redeployment-first handling, early consultation with staff representatives, and clear criteria distinguishing role change from redundancy. A workforce impact assessment sits alongside data protection and equality impact assessments as a mandatory approval gate. Policy commits that released time is first reinvested in care quality and backlog before any headcount decision. Staff representatives are involved from design stage, not at notice stage. Level 4: Manage. Transitions are measured and managed. Redeployment success, equality impact, and whether predicted savings actually materialised are all tracked and reported. Redeployment rates and post-transition retention are tracked by staff group. Equality impact of role changes is analysed by protected characteristic and acted on where disparities appear. Post-implementation review tests whether claimed savings were realised or merely displaced elsewhere. Level 5: Orchestrate. Workforce transition is orchestrated across the health system, using attrition and reskilling rather than displacement, and creating the new roles that AI itself requires. A regional employer network shares redeployment opportunities so staff move between organisations rather than out of the sector. New roles such as AI assurance specialist, clinical safety officer, and prompt and evaluation engineer are created and funded. The organisation publishes its workforce transition evidence so others can plan on real data rather than vendor claims. Notes on scope Redundancies in this model means workforce reduction and role change arising from AI adoption. Operational redundancy in the engineering sense, meaning failover and fallback when a system or model is unavailable, is covered under Software high availability and Software disaster recovery . System leadership sections assess the leadership of a constituency, not the seniority of individuals. An organisation can employ excellent clinicians and still score level 1 on system leadership of medical practitioners if none of them has a mandate, protected time, or a governance route. Digital sovereignty is scored on demonstrated control and evidenced portability, not on stated preference. A contract clause requiring in-country storage is level 2 evidence; a rehearsed provider switch is level 5 evidence. Software sections are grouped together near the top of the model because they progress together. An organisation rarely reaches level 4 in Software DevOps while remaining at level 1 in Software architecture , and a mismatch between them is usually worth investigating. Apps and websites sections are split by audience because the safety, accessibility, and disclosure obligations differ sharply between patients and providers. headings: Gartner's Enterprise Information Management Maturity Model
records.text: Gartner's Enterprise Information Management Maturity Model See The Gartner's EIM Program Maturity Model Level 0 : Unaware Business and IT do net know that information is a problem, while users mistrust the data. Organisation runs significant risk from under managed information, such as compliances failures, poor customer service and productivity. Level 1 : Aware Some awareness of the importance of Information Strategy and Data Governance. Organisation understand the need for common standards, tools and models. Minimal investment in people, process and technology; lack of business sponsorship and involvement. Effort to document risk associated with uncontrolled information assets has begun. Awareness is growing poor data quality and of fragmented and inconsistent information in key subject areas. IT departments seek efficiencies through vertical silo consolidation (Data Warehouse) using data modellers and databases administrators BI continue generating inconsistent or redundant reports. Level 2 : Reactive Emerging Information Management (IM) Strategy & Roadmap, Governance and Processes. Organisation takes steps toward cross-department sharing to actieve operational efficiency. Investments are being made to uplift IM capabilities in some areas. Risks of not managing information as corporate asset are well understood. Metrics are emerging to focus on retention for information, files, email. etc. to address known security and compliance risks. IM Polices and Standards are published, but adherence and compliance are still low. Essential elements of well-architected Data Warehouse (DW)/Business Intelligence (BI) framework / technology are emerging. Level 3 : Proactive Strategy & Roadmap, Governance and Processes are in place enabling proactive IM. Full business sponsorship and involvement, promoting enterprise-wide initiatives. Organisation sets standards for IM technology: distinct architecture for Analytics, Enterprise Data Management, Federated DW/BI unified at the business level - information as a service (Information service layer & Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA). Full compliance with IM Policies and Standards. Operational risk is minimised: IM is embedded in SDLC as projects are implemented and Governance Committees with Information Owners and Information Stewards help manage information as an asset. Level 4 : Managed Senior Management in Business and IT recognises Informaticsn as a strategic asset, embraces and funds Enterprise Information Management (EIM) Program that adresses key stakeholders, requirements and aligned with priorities based on the business strategy. Consistent and mature governance, policies, procedures and EIM operating model ensures coordination of all IM activities. Best practices are identified, and EIM teem ensures that these are extended across the enterprise. Corporate performance is managed by DW/BI dashboards and scorecards. Level 5 Effective Senior management sees information as a compettive advantage and exploits it to create value and increase efficiency. Enterprise Data is managed as a strategic asset across the entire value chain - effectively, ethically and efficiently. EIM Group coordinates all information efforts across the enterprise.. Organisation strives to make IM more transparent to both Business and Technology organisations, with business-level data owners and stewards playing active roles. The orgarnisation has achieved its EIM goals. Useful links EIM Dimensions Gartner's webinar

records.text: Great Professional Service Firms - by Tom Peters See http://tompeters.com/docs/GREAT PSFs 0820 12.pdf Stunning commitment to integrity. Counselors/trusted advisors first. We are not in a commodity business. Stellar listeners—to our Clients. Stellar listeners—to our fellow partners. Stellar listeners—to our most junior associates. (!!!!!) Stellar listeners—to every member of staff. Insatiable curiosity marks 100% of us. We live to serve/Extreme Service ethic. Our leaders are servant leaders. (Every partner is a leader/servant leader first.) Deeply ingrained sense of fairness. Hustlers—but thoughtful to a fault! (Excise rude bastards.) “Service ethic” means service to one another as much as service to clients. Drop everything to assist a colleague in need—central to our overall ethos. A compensation scheme that unmistakably and visibly and dramatically rewards partner cooperation in developing and serving and retaining clients. Toss “lousy colleagues” (bad teammates) out on their derrieres (asses). We will not tolerate less than class-A supportiveness; we will toss out top “rainmakers” who do not subscribe to our abiding teamwork ethic. Intellectual point of view that is Distinct/Exciting. We listen intently, but we also push our clients to explore significantly new approaches to doing business. We insist, as best we can, that every client consider and test discontinuous change. We understand that implementing our advice may require “culture change” in the client’s operation; we will leave a practical framework-process behind to help the client embrace and execute such excruciatingly difficult change. We will stretch our clients to the limits—but not suggest actions that are beyond the reach of implementation in the mid-term future. (“Never give an order that cannot be obeyed.”—MacArthur.) We will intimately assist the client in achieving near-term “small wins” that signify and exemplify the changes the client intends to embrace. Every partner must have a point of view of note—and a point of view that is recognised far beyond our firm’s borders. The definition of the very best partners is that they are “insanely great” mentors! (thanks, Steve Jobs) Equal compensation/recognition to top “rainmakers,” “intellectuals,” and “magical mentors.” We are all “rainmakers”—responsible for making it clear to the client that he/she made a great decision in associating with us. Invest heavily in ideas—this means significant time and $$$$$$$. Invest heavily in training and retraining. (Our training will feature working with clients to implement our ideas, the managerial aspect of directing client engagements, the theory and art and practice of leadership, listening and presenting and understanding the “business principles” that are essential to our economic survival.) (I.e., clients that lead us-drag us into new pastures.) A clear understanding that the “middle market” is often the key to success and vitality—we will not be conned by some specious/ego-centric need to be associated with the likes of the “Fortune 100.” Willingness to dump bad-demotivating-enervating clients (even big ones). (Yes, damn it.) (Make it a fun place to work—David Ogilvy.) Professional to a fault (we love the word “professional”) ... but not pompous. “d”iversity—diversity of every flavor one can imagine. (This is huge and often honored in the breech.) Notable-visible respect for the ideas of young associates. (!!) Practice-as-teamwork. (Teammate-ism rewarded, lack thereof punished with extreme prejudice.) Deep bench. “Supporting cast,” notably starting with receptionist, must be of same quality as partners—there are no “bit players” in our business. Age gracefully gives way to youth—regeneration a deep-seated guiding belief. Youth gracefully gives way to age—our most effective elders have much to teach us when, especially, it comes to client retention. Hard work expected and cherished—workaholism for workaholism’s sake assiduously guarded against. Proud of our culture, guard our culture zealously—but even “great cultures” age. (And at the least become horribly elaborated.) Rigorous evaluations of client satisfaction by more or less disinterested parties. Sky-high time investment in our evaluation process. My legacy (as a partner) is: Being of service. Developing people. Being a good colleague—which absorbed lots of my time. Doing consistently superior (sky high) quality work. Adding materially to the ideas base of the Firm. Insuring the continuity of the firm—culturally and financially. Being a paragon of integrity and decency. Leaving gracefully. “Execution is strategy.” (Thanks, Fred Malek.) My word is my bond. Wow! (Aspiration for every assignment? Right? Why not? What else?) Excellence! PERIOD! (Why not? records.title: Hype as a scale
records.text: Hype as a scale https://johannesklingebiel.de/2022/01/12/hype-as-a-scale.html Level 1: Marketing Claims This is your standard marketing speak. They‘re focused on what existing technology can do for you almost immediately. Though exaggerated, they‘re still grounded in reality. Marketing claims work on an immediate time scale, meaning whatever they promise can be realised almost instantly. The technology already exists. Level 2: Exaggerated Claims Here the effects and impact of an existing technology are greatly exaggerated and oversold but still informed by its real capabilities. The focus lies on the returns to come by investing now. These claims oversell the present capabilities of a technology, often skirting the line to fraud. A good example might be Tesla selling their driving assistance systems as “full self-driving”. Level 3: Utopian Futures The technology is the key to a utopian future or the avoidance of a dystopic one. Claims are solely focussed on the “potential” of the technology, less its benefits in the present. Here the focus of the hype is solely on the future, though the time-scale is still concrete, promising the technology will arrive at a fixed time from now. One example here might be carbon capture technology, though it already exists in the form of prototypes, it‘s still in its infancy. Thus boosters of the technology will emphasize the future potential of its present capabilities to attract further investment and political support. Level 4: Magical Thinking The technology has left grounded reality and takes on magical properties. The problems it is expected to solve simply by existing are growing in number and scale while criticism gets ignored as minor hurdles, to be overcome soon. With magical thinking concrete predictions are becoming less and less important, though the development might still be expected at a fixed date. A particularly good example here might be the blockchain industry, which has been overselling the capabilities of the technology for years — pitching it as a solution to every imaginable societal problem and challenge. Level 5: Othering The technology has become a group identity for its boosters. Claims are exclusively utopian, and critics are painted as defenders of the old, to be left behind. This is the most aggressive and annoying form of hype. Notably, the time of arrival is less important at this level, simply that the technology will arrive at some point in the future. Examples here are (again) the cryptocurrency scene which has been pretty good at othering critics as “no-coiners” or lately with the phrase “have fun staying poor”. Another example might also be particularly vocal groups of boosters at the height of the AI hype a couple of years ago. Here the claims were that critics simply didn’t “understand exponential growth”.

records.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) maturity model by Joel Parker Henderson
headings: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) maturity model by Joel Parker Henderson
records.text: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) maturity model by Joel Parker Henderson Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the process of managing and provisioning computing infrastructure (processes, bare-metal servers, virtual servers, etc.) and their configuration through machine-processable files (source code, scripts, declarative files, dotfiles, etc.) rather than physical hardware configuration or the use of interactive tools. See Wikipedia: Infrastructure as Code Continuous configuration automatiion (CCA) DevOps Maturity model Level 0: None No IaC, or negligible use, or not applicable. Level 1: Initial + Informal Infrastructure as Code is in initial stages, including areas such as assessments, a trial project, a pilot, a prototype. Teammates on a project are starting to talking about IaC, typically with one hero or small group of people who want it. Code quality of the IaC code tends to be hand-rolled, or hand-tested, or hand-tooled. Application planning focuses on shipping code. Examples: Use cloud services, such as Amazon Web Services. Use a shell script that check a server's uptime Ideas to improve: Shift from using hand-rolled one-off installations toward using package managers such as apm, apt, brew, choco melpa, gem, pip, yum, as well as configuration management such as config files and dot files. Learn about any popular mainstream configuration tools, such as Ansible, Salt, Puppet, Chef. Level 2: Developing + Describing Infrastructure is developing, typically because of a team's need. Typical software at this level often includes cloud services (e.g. AWS), containerization (e.g. Docker), configuration management (e.g. Ansible), orchestration tooling (e.g. Kubernetes), continuous delivery software (e.g. GoCD), and potentially platform as a service offerings (e.g. Heroku). Teammates from the department are talking about IaC, and working on ways to use IaC to help the department across multiple projects. Code quality is starting to use automated tests for the IaC code, in addition to application code. IaC proponents develop and describe cross-functional areas, such as Cost (reduction), Speed (execution), and Risk (mitigation). Application planning includes documentation, ideally orienting toward developing various cookbooks, recipies, manifests, blueprints, as well as developer operations (devops) such as continuous integration, deployment pipelines as an integral part of the application delivery process, and quality assurance that covers the entire delivery pipeline. Examples: There are at least a few projects where a developer can commit a line of code, and the code flows into production, by using continuous integration, continuous delivery, and optionally capabilities for feature flags, throttle releases (blue/green, go/no, canary releases, etc.). The department shares IaC code and does IaC collaboration using source code repositories, and optionally capabilities for chat, help, documentation, wikis, planning, and the like. Ideas to improve: Technical: Develop IaC code in ways that align with your teams' project code, such as doing code reviews, roadmap planning, idempotency testing, etc. Get familiar with all of the examples above: AWS, Docker, Ansible, Kubernetes, GoCD, Heroku; even if you choose to use alternatives to these, the learning will transfer well. Social: Share IaC code with other teams, get feedback, and improve the code and all its related capabilities for collaboration, documentation, verification, etc. Level 3: Standardising + Scaling Infrastructure is standardising, typically thanks to teams creating specifications, sharable code, source code repositories. Team members can quickly, confidently, and effectively create IaC projects, complete with end-to-end success, as well as any documentation and certification. Code quality aims toward service-oriented capabilities, such as APIs, discoverability, mixability. The approach to IaC is generally imperative and/or procedural. The imperative approach focuses on how the infrastructure is to be changed to meet the target configuration. The imperative approach defines specific commands that need to be executed to end with the desired conclusion. IaC proponents standardise cross-functional areas, such as Cost (reduction), Speed (execution), and Risk (mitigation). The standardisation incldues specific tradeoffs, such as the cost/benefit of faster deployments, or the risk/reward of security verfications. Application planning includes design for self-standardisation and/or self-scaling, as well as devops techniques such as immutable infrastructure, phoenix servers, IaaS, PaaS, and iPaaS. Examples: Typically projects can be one-button deployed, including just-in-time as-needed creation of related resources, databases, networks, addresses, etc. IaC is in use beyond just the IT department; this may include self-service tools, such as setting up new laptops, as well as significant business tools, such as IT-business teams that can configure and deploy new services independently of IT system administrators. How to improve: Technical: Learn how to modularize Iac code and distribute it, such as by using package managers, modules, libraries, functional decomposition, idempotency testing, hot reloads, etc. Social: Explicity plan for good governance. Governance includes technical areas such as versioning and release management, team areas such as five-why root cause analysis and blameless retrospectives, and management areas such as budgeting and approvals. Level 4: Managing + Measuring + Missions Infrastructure is managed and measured in concert with explicit mission statements. Good candidates are OKRs (Objectives and Key Results), KPI (Key Performance Indicator) metrics, and a Strategic Balanced Scorecard. Team members can easily use scoreboards, dashboards, metrics, measurments, and similar data-driven tooling to run, upgrade, and verify IaC code. IT executive leadership can easily use rollup systems to prove IT-business capabilities and cost justifications. Code quality is consistently measured and tested using continuous delivery tooling, automated code quality vetting, scaling benchmarking, etc. The approach to IaC is generally declarative and/or functional. The declarative approach focuses on what the eventual target configuration should be. The declarative approach defines the desired state, and the system executes what needs to happen to achieve that desired state. IaC proponents prove success in cross-functional areas, such as Cost (reduction), Speed (execution), and Risk (mitigation). The proof includes data for cost/benefit of faster deployments, risk/reward of security verifications, etc. Application planning includes design for self-management and/or self-measurement. Examples: Many projects are one-button initiated, end-to-end, from sunrise to sunset. This can include Application Lifcycle Management (ALM), Porfolio Programme Project Management (PPPM), best practices, maturity model matching, etc. IaC tooling emits metrics, which in turn are useful for Application Performance Monitoring (APM), synthetic monitoring, debugging, and capability growth planning. How to improve: Technical: improve code so it's suitable for mainstream usage. This includes thorough test coverage for corner cases, failure modes, chaos interruptions, outage mitigations. Social: Plan IaC in terms of long-term management and mainstream usage, including roadmaps for lifecycle management, funding management, communication management, value stream mapping, and governance management. Level 5: Optimising + Orchestrating + Opportunities Infrastructure research and development is funded to create new products and services, and also new business opportunities. Code quality is consistently able evolve, and welcomes contributions, discussions, and usage by the entire organisation, and potentially its partners, vendors, customers, and the public. The approach to IaC is orchestral and environmentatlly aware. The orchestral approach focuses on why the configuration should be a certain way in consideration of all the co-relationships and co-dependencies of multiple applications running on the same infrastructure typically found in production. IaC proponents optimise success in cross-functional areas, such as Cost (reduction), Speed (execution), and Risk (mitigation). The optimisation includes data for cost/benefit of faster deployments, risk/reward of security verifications, etc. The optimisation also includes strategic look-ahead to drive organisational investment in these cross-functional areas. Application planning includes design for self-optimisation and/or self-healing. Examples: Amazon creating AWS, Google creating GCS, Facebook creating React, Netflix creating many open source projects. Orchestrating among multiple clouds, internal and external, with tools such as Kubernetes and Mesos. How to improve: Create code that inspires people to grow more IaC capabilities. This includes publicizing the code, such as blogging about it, creating help channels for it, and teaching how to use it. Use IT to drive strategic opportunities, such as investments in companies, products, and people.
